briefs.cyanotic-chd:
Congenital Heart Disease

cyanotic lesions · left-to-right shunts · their timing: weeks for shunts, days for the ductusWhen did it declare, and which structure makes the murmur?

WorkupCyanotic lesionsShuntsPractice
Bottom line

Sort by when it declares (birth, infancy, spells) and the murmur (present or absent, and its source).

  • A murmur needs a pressure gradient: when one appears or fades, the gradient changed.
  • Left-to-right shunts declare over weeks, as pulmonary vascular resistance falls.
  • Ductal-dependent lesions declare over days, as the ductus closes.
  • Silent cyanosis: total anomalous pulmonary venous return or hypoplastic left heart syndrome.
  • Tet spell: the outflow obstruction is partly dynamic; crying or dehydration can tighten it (the trigger is not fully understood), or a drop in systemic vascular resistance (SVR) lets more blood shunt right to left; squatting or knee-chest raises SVR and aborts it.
Workup
Cyanotic lesions
Mechanism, then the tell
LesionMechanismThe tell
Total anomalous pulmonary venous returnPulmonary veins drain to the right heartBirth; no murmur, at most soft pulmonic flow
Hypoplastic left heart syndromeTiny left ventricle, absent mitral and aortic valves; lives on the ductus and atrial defectBirth; no murmur
Tricuspid atresiaNo right atrium to right ventricle path; atrial defect plus a ventricular defect or ductusBirth; ventricular defect or ductal murmur, or both
Truncus arteriosusOne arterial trunk over a ventricular septal defectTypically infancy, not birth; holosystolic murmur
Tetralogy of FallotOutflow narrowing pushes blood right to left across a large ventricular septal defectHarsh systolic, left upper sternal border; fades in a spell
Ebstein anomalyTricuspid valve displaced apically; atrialized right ventricleTricuspid regurgitation, widely split S1 (first heart sound), sail sound; severe: birth
Tetralogy PROVe – Pulmonic stenosis (right ventricular (RV) outflow obstruction), RV hypertrophy, Overriding aorta, VSD (ventricular septal defect) · Murmur – from the narrowed outflow tract; the defect is too large to make one · Spectrum – severe narrowing, cyanotic at birth; milder, spells in infancy · 5 Ts – Truncus, Transposition, Tricuspid atresia, Tetralogy, Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
Left-to-right shunts and the transitional clock
Acyanotic lesions
LesionThe tellThen
Ventricular septal defectHolosystolic, lower sternal border; louder means smallerDiurese and feed; close if failure persists
Atrial septal defectFixed split S2 (second heart sound), soft pulmonic flow murmurOften silent into childhood; no cyanosis
Patent ductus arteriosusContinuous machine-like, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressurePreterm: indomethacin or ibuprofen closes it; murmur disappears
Coarctation of the aortaArm-leg pressure gap, weak femoral pulsesDays: PGE1 reopens the ductus
Prostaglandin opens, indomethacin closes Ductal-dependent – coarctation, pulmonary atresia, transposition, hypoplastic left heart decompensate as the ductus closes: reopen it · Preterm ductus – shunting into the lungs is the problem: close it · Softening murmur – in an unrepaired large shunt, a warning, not an improvement
Practice
  1. 5-week-old boy, born at term, had a normal 2-week visit now feeds poorly and breathes fast new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Murmur absent on the newborn examination Afebrile · respiratory rate 70/min · acyanotic → Pulmonary vascular resistance has fallen → at birth pulmonary vascular resistance is near systemic, so almost nothing crosses the defect; as it falls, the gradient opens, the murmur appears at 2 to 4 weeks, and the same overcirculation causes the tachypnea and poor feeding. The ductus was already closed by the normal 2-week visit, and its closure removes a continuous murmur rather than creating a holosystolic one; rising pulmonary pressure would soften the murmur
  2. 1-day-old boy has been cyanotic since birth no murmur echocardiogram shows the pulmonary veins draining to the right atrium Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 80% on room air · HR 160/min → Total anomalous pulmonary venous return → pulmonary veins draining to the right heart give cyanosis at birth with no murmur, at most a soft pulmonic flow murmur; tetralogy has a harsh outflow murmur, and truncus arteriosus has a holosystolic murmur with cyanosis typically arriving in infancy
  3. 6-week-old boy was diagnosed with a large ventricular septal defect at 2 weeks poor weight gain liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin Feeds tire him Afebrile · respiratory rate 70/min → Diuretics, afterload reduction and caloric fortification → heart failure from a left-to-right shunt arrives at 4 to 6 weeks; failure to thrive is the infant form of exercise intolerance. Diurese and feed first, and close the defect if failure persists: observation leaves the failure untreated, and surgery comes after medical therapy fails
  4. 4-month-old boy has episodes of deep cyanosis while crying episodes resolve when he is held with knees to chest harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border Afebrile · oxygen saturation 84% between episodes → Tetralogy of Fallot → right ventricular outflow tract obstruction drives right-to-left flow across a large ventricular septal defect, and knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance to reverse it; truncus arteriosus gives a holosystolic murmur without spells, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return has no murmur
  5. 1-day-old girl has a normal examination before discharge fails her pulse oximetry screen at 24 hours Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; feeding well Afebrile · HR 140/min · BP 70/42 mm Hg → Echocardiography → a failed screen means possible critical congenital heart disease, and only echocardiography names the anatomy; a chest radiograph only supports, and repeating a failed screen delays the study
  6. 1-day-old girl has been cyanotic since birth no murmur echocardiogram shows a severely underdeveloped left ventricle Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 82% on room air · HR 166/min → Prostaglandin E1 infusion → the ductus and the atrial defect are the only route to the systemic circulation, so the shunts must stay open: prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open; indomethacin closes it, and oxygen alone leaves it to close over days
  7. 3-week-old girl is seen for a weight check fixed splitting of S2 soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border Thriving and gaining weight Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% on room air → Atrial septal defect → a fixed split S2 with a soft pulmonic flow murmur and no cyanosis is an atrial septal defect; the atrial gradient stays low, so it is often silent into childhood. A ventricular septal defect is holosystolic at the lower sternal border, and a patent ductus is continuous and machine-like
  8. 2-month-old boy was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth deeply cyanotic while crying improves when his mother holds his knees to his chest Afebrile · oxygen saturation 62% while crying, 84% after → Increased systemic vascular resistance reduces right-to-left shunting → knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance, which reverses the right-to-left shunt; the lever is systemic vascular resistance, not venous return or the coronary circulation
  9. 2-month-old girl is evaluated for a murmur holosystolic tricuspid regurgitation murmur at the left lower sternal border widely split S1 early systolic sail sound Feeding and growing well Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on room air → Ebstein anomaly → apical displacement of the tricuspid valve atrializes the right ventricle and makes the regurgitation murmur, the widely split S1 and the sail sound; tricuspid atresia has no right atrium to right ventricle path, and pulmonic stenosis makes an outflow murmur
  10. 4-month-old girl was diagnosed with a large ventricular septal defect at 1 month never repaired murmur has softened now desaturates with crying Parents say the quieter murmur means it is closing Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% at rest → Urgent cardiology referral → a softening murmur in an unrepaired large shunt is a warning, not an improvement: pulmonary vascular resistance is rising and the shunt is starting to reverse, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome ⚠︎; refer urgently while repair is still possible. Reassurance reads it as closure; an afterload reducer with a 3-month recheck treats overcirculation that is already reversing and delays repair
  11. 1-day-old boy has been cyanotic since birth holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border ECG shows left axis deviation with small right ventricular forces No spells with crying Afebrile · oxygen saturation 78% on room air → Tricuspid atresia → with no right atrium to right ventricle path, flow depends on the atrial defect plus a ventricular defect or ductus, whose murmur is heard; left axis deviation with small right ventricular forces is its ECG. Tetralogy has right ventricular hypertrophy and an outflow murmur. Ebstein, cyanotic at birth when severe, also gives a regurgitation murmur, but adds a widely split S1, a sail sound and a massive box-shaped heart; left axis with small right ventricular forces is the tricuspid atresia ECG
  12. 2-day-old boy is pale and mottled weak femoral pulses right arm blood pressure 30 mm Hg above the leg In shock on arrival Afebrile · BP 86/50 mm Hg in the right arm · HR 190/min → Start prostaglandin E1 → coarctation declares in days, as the ductus closes: prostaglandin E1 reopens it. Diuretics and a fluid bolus leave the closing ductus untouched
  13. 2-month-old boy has cyanosis that began in recent weeks holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a single arterial trunk over a large defect in the ventricular septum Afebrile · oxygen saturation 86% → Truncus arteriosus → a single shared arterial trunk over a ventricular septal defect gives cyanosis characteristically in infancy, not at birth, with a holosystolic murmur; tetralogy has a harsh outflow murmur and spells, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return has no murmur
  14. 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with a ventricular septal defect at 2 weeks loud grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a small defect Afebrile · weight at the 50th percentile → A small defect produces high-velocity turbulent flow → a small defect makes high-velocity turbulent flow; large defects are quieter and shunt more, so murmur intensity runs opposite to severity. A loud murmur reflects a high gradient, not a high right ventricular pressure, which would soften it
  15. 3-month-old girl has episodes of deeper cyanosis with crying episodes resolve when she is calm harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border Afebrile · baseline oxygen saturation 86% → Echocardiography → echocardiography confirms the ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta and narrowed outflow tract; a chest radiograph (boot-shaped heart) and an ECG only support
  16. 3-day-old preterm boy born at 28 weeks continuous murmur below the left clavicle bounding pulses widened pulse pressure Murmur first heard today on rounds Afebrile · BP 58/24 mm Hg · respiratory rate 64/min → Indomethacin or ibuprofen → a hemodynamically significant preterm ductus (bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, tachypnea) shunting into the lungs is the problem, so close it with indomethacin or ibuprofen; prostaglandin E1 keeps a ductus open, and observation alone leaves the shunt in place
  17. 1-day-old boy with Down syndrome has mild cyanosis with feeds fixed split S2 grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Born at term after an uncomplicated delivery Afebrile · oxygen saturation 90% during feeds → Complete atrioventricular canal defect → an atrial sign (fixed split S2) and a lower-sternal-border murmur, with cyanosis, in Down syndrome: echocardiography defines it. An isolated ventricular or atrial septal defect shunts left to right and causes no cyanosis. On day 1 pulmonary vascular resistance is still near systemic, so little crosses left to right yet
  18. 3-day-old girl has cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen single S2 now weak pulses with poor perfusion Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; feeding poorly today Afebrile · oxygen saturation 70% on 100% oxygen · HR 190/min → Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiography → unchanged saturation on 100% oxygen is a fixed shunt, not lung disease; weak pulses mean the ductus is closing, so instability licenses prostaglandin E1 before the picture; waiting for echocardiography or adding oxygen lets it close
  19. 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border echocardiogram shows a large ventricular septal defect and an overriding aorta Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% → Flow through the narrowed RV outflow tract → the ventricular septal defect is real anatomy but too large to generate a murmur; the murmur comes from the narrowed right ventricular (RV) outflow tract, and the overriding aorta adds none
  20. 6-week-old boy has fed poorly for 1 week tachypneic and acyanotic holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Murmur absent on the newborn examination; born at term Afebrile · respiratory rate 68/min · oxygen saturation 98% → Ventricular septal defect → a holosystolic lower-sternal-border murmur in an acyanotic infant is a ventricular septal defect, appearing as pulmonary vascular resistance falls; an atrial septal defect gives a fixed split S2 and is often silent into childhood, and a patent ductus is continuous
How NBME framed it: question 1

3-month-old boy brought to the emergency department with 3 days of pallor, low-grade fever, vomiting, occasional diarrhea and poor feeding Mildly dehydrated and cyanotic; perfusion and muscle tone normal T 37.8 °C · pulse 165/min · respirations 35/min · BP 80/48 mm Hg · oxygen saturation 85% on room air harsh grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur over the whole precordium cries and becomes agitated as an intravenous catheter is attempted saturation then drops to 60% and the murmur is barely audible Supplemental oxygen is given

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Atrial septal defect: a common defect with a systolic murmur; but it shunts left to right with a fixed split S2 and causes no cyanosis.
  • Coarctation of the aorta: a can't-miss lesion in an ill infant; but it gives arm hypertension, weak leg pulses and lower leg pressures, not cyanotic spells.
  • Ventricular septal defect: a harsh murmur in an infant; but an isolated defect is holosystolic and acyanotic; a murmur that fades as cyanosis develops over months means rising resistance reversing the shunt, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome ⚠︎, not an acute spell with crying.

Down to two: tetralogy of Fallot or pulmonary stenosis. Tetralogy of Fallot: isolated pulmonary stenosis makes a similar outflow murmur, but with no ventricular septal defect it causes no cyanotic spells with crying. Crying tightens the outflow obstruction (the trigger is not fully understood), pulmonary flow drops, and less flow makes a softer murmur. The stem reads like a febrile stomach illness; the witnessed spell names the lesion, and the oxygen given treats the number, not the shunt.

Common wrong answers Give oxygen in a spell: the shunt is anatomic; SVR, not inspired oxygen, is the lever. Flow across the ventricular septal defect: real anatomy, wrong source of the tetralogy murmur. Ductal closure: removes a continuous murmur, cannot create a holosystolic one. Rising pulmonary pressure: the opposite direction; it would soften the murmur.
Pairs with Part I Heart Murmurs in a Child: central cyanosis and a single or fixed S2 are pathologic; ask, cyanosis at birth, and is there a murmur? Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn: the sort to finish first. Part II Murmur Man and Post-ToF Pulmonic Regurgitation: murmur shape and location. Part II Neonatal Respiratory Distress: lung versus heart.
Transferable rule

Time it, then hear it: when did cyanosis or the murmur arrive, and which structure makes the sound? A murmur that appears or fades means the gradient changed, not the heart.
